items.prompt: What does the abbreviation WCAG stand for?

options.label: Web Compatibility and Access Grammar
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines
World Convention for Accessible Graphics
Website Code Accessibility Group

rubric: WCAG is the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines published by the W3C.
Other options are plausible-sounding invented expansions.

items.prompt: Which HTML attribute supplies a text alternative for an `` element?

options.label: `alt`
`src`
`rel`
`lang`

rubric: The `alt` attribute holds the text alternative read by screen readers.
`src` only points to the file; `lang` and `rel` serve other purposes.

items.prompt: What is the minimum contrast ratio WCAG level AA requires for normal-size body text against its background?
rubric: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text.
3:1 applies to large text and 7:1 is the stricter AAA level.

items.prompt: Which HTML element marks a block of main site navigation links as a navigation landmark?

options.label: `<nav>`
`<menu>`
`<header>`
`<aside>`

rubric: `<nav>` exposes a navigation landmark to assistive technology.
`<header>` and `<aside>` are other landmarks; `<menu>` is not a navigation landmark.

items.prompt: Which keyboard key is normally used to move focus to the next interactive element on a page?

options.label: Escape
Space
Enter
Tab

rubric: Tab moves focus forward; Shift+Tab moves back.
Enter and Space activate controls; Escape dismisses things.

items.prompt: Which of these elements are focusable with the keyboard by default, without adding `tabindex`? Select all that apply.

options.label: `<button>`
`<a href="/home">`
`<div>`
`<input type="text">`

rubric: Buttons, links with href and form inputs are natively focusable.

`

` and `

` are not focusable unless given `tabindex`.

items.prompt: A developer builds a toolbar button that shows only a magnifier icon and no visible text. A screen reader currently announces it just as "button". Which attribute should the developer add to give it an accessible name?

options.label: `tabindex="-1"`
`role="presentation"`
`aria-label="Search"`
`aria-hidden="true"`

rubric: `aria-label` provides an accessible name for icon-only controls.
The other attributes hide the control or remove it from tab order, making things worse.

items.prompt: Why should a page use heading elements (`<h1>` to `<h6>`) in a logical order instead of styling `<div>` text to look like headings?

options.label: Browsers render real heading elements faster than styled divs, which helps users on slow connections
Search engines mostly skip text outside heading tags, so styled divs can hurt a page's ranking
Screen reader users can jump between headings to navigate the page
Headings are the main way to change font size in a way that respects user zoom settings

rubric: Headings create a navigable outline for assistive technology.
Distractors claim performance or styling benefits that are not the accessibility reason.

items.prompt: A form marks invalid fields only by turning their border red. Why does this fail some users?

options.label: Colour-blind users and screen reader users may not perceive colour alone
Red borders on a white page always fall below the minimum contrast ratio for text
Browsers drop border styling when users zoom the page, so the error marker disappears
Accessibility rules forbid red for error states because it is reserved for browser warnings

rubric: Colour must not be the only means of conveying information.
Distractors invent rules about red or borders.

items.prompt: What is the effect of `aria-hidden="true"` on a visible element?

options.label: It removes the element from the accessibility tree but leaves it visible
It deletes the element from the DOM once the page has finished loading
It hides the element visually, but screen readers still read its content
It disables the element so it cannot be focused or receive clicks

rubric: `aria-hidden` removes the element from the accessibility tree only.
Distractors reverse the effect or confuse it with disabling or removal.

items.prompt: Why is it a problem to add `outline: none` to links and buttons without providing another focus style?

options.label: Browsers stop applying any other CSS to those elements
Keyboard users can't see which element has focus
Mouse users can no longer click the elements reliably
Screen readers stop announcing the elements as links

rubric: A visible focus indicator shows keyboard users where they are.
Distractors link outlines to mouse clicks or screen reader output, which they do not control.

items.prompt: Why do accessibility guidelines advise using a native `<button>` rather than a `<div role="button">`?

options.label: A div with a role cannot be announced by any screen reader
ARIA roles are deprecated and ignored by browsers
A native button always looks better without any CSS
A native button is built in with keyboard support and semantics, so no extra scripting is needed

rubric: Native elements bring focus, Enter/Space activation and semantics for free.
Distractors wrongly claim ARIA roles do not work or that looks matter.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe good practice for image alt text? Select all that apply.

options.label: Alt text should convey what a linked image does, such as where the link goes
Purely decorative images get an empty `alt=""` so screen readers skip them
Alt text should start with "image of" so users know it is a picture
Informative images get alt text describing their purpose or content
Alt text should include extra keywords to help search ranking

rubric: Alt text conveys purpose; decorative images use empty alt; linked images describe the destination or action.
"Image of" is redundant since screen readers announce images, and keyword stuffing harms users.

items.prompt: A sign-up form shows an email field with only a placeholder reading "Email address". Screen reader users report that once they start typing, they do not know what the field is for. What best explains the problem and its fix?

options.label: The placeholder text is too short to be announced, so lengthen it to describe the expected format
Screen readers skip input fields without a visible border, so add a CSS outline to the field
The placeholder is read only when the field is hidden, so add aria-hidden="true" to the input
Placeholders vanish and are no real label, so add a <label> linked by for and id

rubric: Placeholders vanish and are not a substitute for a programmatically associated label.
Distractors suggest lengthening the placeholder or hiding the field, which does not give it a name.

items.prompt: Why is a `<button>` usually better than a `<div onclick="...">` for a clickable control?

options.label: A div cannot receive click events in browsers unless it has a role attribute
A div cannot be styled with CSS to look like a button without extra markup
A button is focusable and activates with Enter and Space by default
A button is announced more loudly by screen readers than a plain div is

rubric: Native buttons provide keyboard focus, activation and a role without extra code.
Distractors assume divs cannot be clickable or styled, which is false; the real gap is built-in semantics and keyboard support.

items.prompt: A page has a purely decorative flourish image that adds no information. How should its `alt` be handled?

options.label: Set `alt="decorative image"` so users know to skip it
Set `title` to the file name so assistive tech can find it
Leave out the `alt` attribute so screen readers ignore it
Use an empty `alt=""` so screen readers skip the image

rubric: An empty alt marks the image as decorative so it is skipped.
A missing alt often leads screen readers to read the file name, a common misconception.

items.prompt: Under WCAG AA, what is the minimum contrast ratio for normal-size body text against its background?
rubric: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text.
3:1 applies to large text and UI components; 7:1 is the AAA level.

items.prompt: Why is a `placeholder` attribute not a good replacement for a visible `<label>` on a text input?

options.label: Placeholder text disappears once typing starts, so it is not a persistent name
Screen readers usually read placeholder text twice, which confuses users who rely on them
Placeholders are valid only on password inputs, so other input types need a label
Placeholder text cannot be styled with CSS, so its contrast tends to fall below the WCAG minimum

rubric: Placeholder text disappears while typing and is a weak accessible name, leaving users without context.
Distractors invent technical restrictions that do not exist.

items.prompt: Which statement best captures the first rule of ARIA?

options.label: Use ARIA attributes because they add keyboard behaviour to any element, so native controls are unnecessary
Add ARIA roles to every element so screen readers get maximum detail
Use a native HTML element with the needed semantics instead of ARIA when possible
Replace headings and landmarks with ARIA roles so every screen reader announces them consistently

rubric: Native elements bring role, state and keyboard behaviour; ARIA is a fallback.
Distractors treat ARIA as adding behaviour or as always better, but it only changes semantics.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain why heading elements (`<h1>` to `<h6>`) should be used in order? Select all that apply.

options.label: Screen reader users can navigate by a list of headings to scan the page
Any heading level can be chosen to get the visual size you want, since CSS is ignored by assistive tech
Skipping levels is fine when you want a smaller font size
Heading levels convey the structure and hierarchy of the content

rubric: Headings expose structure and enable navigation by heading.
Choosing levels for appearance is a misconception; size should be set with CSS.

items.prompt: A designer adds `*:focus { outline: none; }` to a stylesheet to remove the 'ugly' box around links and buttons. A keyboard-only user then tabs through the page. What is the main accessibility problem this causes?

options.label: The user cannot see which element currently has focus
The tab order changes so elements are visited randomly
Links and buttons can no longer receive keyboard focus at all
Screen readers stop announcing links and buttons entirely

rubric: Removing the outline hides the focus indicator (WCAG 2.4.7), so sighted keyboard users lose their position.
Focusability, tab order and screen reader output are not changed by outline.

items.prompt: Which markup correctly associates a visible label with a text input so clicking the label focuses the field?

options.label: `<label for="email">Email</label><input name="email">`
`<label>Email</label><input id="email">`
`<label id="email">Email</label><input type="text">`
`<label for="email">Email</label><input id="email">`

rubric: The label's `for` must match the input's `id`.
Distractors match `name` or place `id` on the label, or omit `for`, so no association exists.

items.prompt: Body text at 16px regular weight has a measured contrast ratio of 3.8:1 against its background. What should you do to meet WCAG AA?

options.label: Leave it, since 3:1 is enough for all text on a page
Increase the size to 18px, which makes it count as large text
Darken the text colour until the ratio is at least 4.5:1
Make the text bold, since bold text only needs 3:1

rubric: Normal text needs 4.5:1, so the colours must change.
Large text needs 24px regular or about 18.7px bold; bolding 16px or going to 18px regular does not qualify.

items.prompt: You want to add a skip link for keyboard users. Which implementation works?

options.label:
Put `Skip to main content` first in ``, with `
` further down the page

Put `Skip to main content` first in ``, with `
`

Put `Skip to main content` first in ``, with `
` below it

Put `Skip to main content` as the last element in ``, with `
` above it

rubric: A skip link must come early in tab order and point to an existing id.
Distractors put it last, remove it from focus, or hide it from assistive tech.

items.prompt: You need an icon-only search button containing an SVG magnifier. Which markup gives it an accessible name?

options.label: `<button aria-hidden="true" aria-label="Search"><svg></svg></button>`
`<button aria-label="Search"><svg aria-hidden="true"></svg></button>`
`<button><svg></svg></button>`

`
`

rubric: A native button with aria-label gives a name and keyboard support; the decorative SVG is hidden.
The div lacks keyboard support, the plain button has no name, and aria-hidden on the button hides it.

items.prompt: A custom modal dialog opens when a user presses a 'Settings' button. What focus handling should you implement?

options.label: Move focus to the top of the page, then leave it there on close
Move focus to the dialog but do not restore it on close
Leave focus on the button and rely on the dialog's title
Move focus into the dialog, then return it to the button on close

rubric: Focus should move into the dialog and return to the trigger when it closes.
Other options strand keyboard users outside the dialog or lose their place afterwards.

items.prompt: You must make a custom `<div role="checkbox">` usable by keyboard and assistive tech. Which changes are needed? Select all that apply.

options.label: Add `tabindex="0"` so it can receive keyboard focus
Add `aria-hidden="true"` to reduce clutter for assistive tech
Toggle `aria-checked` and respond to the Space key
Set `tabindex="-1"` to keep the tab order short

rubric: A custom checkbox needs focusability, key handling and an updated aria-checked state.
aria-hidden removes it from assistive tech and tabindex -1 removes it from the tab order.

items.prompt: On a sign-up form, an invalid email currently only turns the input border red after submit. Colour-blind and screen reader users report not noticing the error. Which change best fixes this?

options.label: Darken the red border to a shade with a much higher contrast ratio against the white page background
Thicken the red border and add a small red warning icon with no text next to the email input
Add a `title="Invalid email"` attribute to the input so the error is described when it is focused
Show text 'Enter a valid email', link it with `aria-describedby`, and set `aria-invalid="true"`

rubric: Errors need a text message programmatically linked to the field, not colour alone.
Other options still rely on colour or on attributes that are unreliably exposed.

items.prompt: You must add a close icon button that shows only an "X" symbol drawn by an SVG. Which markup gives screen reader users a correct name for the control?

options.label: `<button title=""><svg aria-hidden="true">...</svg></button>`
``
`<button aria-label="Close"><svg aria-hidden="true">...</svg></button>`

`
`

rubric: A native button with aria-label gives a name and keyboard support; the SVG is hidden as decoration.
Distractors leave the control with no accessible name or use a non-interactive div.

items.prompt: Body text is `#767676` on a white background at 16px regular. Using WCAG AA, which change is needed for this text to pass if the ratio is about 4.5:1?

options.label: Increase to 24px, since AA needs large text for 4.5:1
None; 4.5:1 meets the AA minimum for normal text
Switch to 3:1 pairing, since AA applies 3:1 to all body text
Darken it to reach 7:1, since AA requires 7:1 for normal text

rubric: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text, so this passes.
7:1 is AAA; 3:1 applies only to large text and UI components.

items.prompt: A form has an input for email next to the text "Email address" in a `<span>`. Which fix correctly associates the label so clicking it focuses the input and screen readers announce it?

options.label: Add `title="Email address"` to the input and wrap the span in a `<div>` placed directly before it
Add `tabindex="0"` to the span and `role="label"` so keyboard users can reach the text and it names the input
Replace the span with `<label for="email">` and set `id="email"` on the input
Add `placeholder="Email address"` to the input and keep the span as visible text beside it

rubric: A label with for/id gives a programmatic name and a larger click target.
Placeholder and title are unreliable names; tabindex on a span doesn't associate it.

items.prompt: You build a custom "Skip to main content" link for keyboard users. Which implementation works correctly?

options.label: `<a href="#main">` placed in the footer, after all of the page content, so it is the last tab stop
`<a href="#main" tabindex="-1">` placed at the top of the page, so it is first in the DOM
First focusable `<a href="#main">` targeting `<main id="main">`, visible on focus
`<a href="#main" style="display:none">` placed at the top of the page, so it is first in the DOM

rubric: The link must be first in tab order, target an element, and be visible on focus.
display:none and tabindex -1 remove it from keyboard use; footer placement defeats the purpose.

items.prompt: A decorative flourish image sits between sections and adds no information. Which markup is correct?

options.label: ``
``
``
``

rubric: Empty alt tells screen readers to skip the image.
A missing alt may cause the filename to be read; descriptive alt adds noise.

items.prompt: Which changes make a custom `<div>`-based toggle switch operable for keyboard and screen reader users? Select all that apply.

options.label: Add `tabindex="0"` and handle Space (and Enter) key presses
Add `role="switch"` and keep `aria-checked` in sync with state
Add `outline: none` so focus rings don't clutter the design
Add `aria-hidden="true"` so it does not confuse screen readers

rubric: Role, state and keyboard handling make a custom control usable.
aria-hidden removes it from assistive tech; removing outlines hides focus.

items.prompt: You open a modal dialog when the user clicks "Settings". The modal contains a heading, form fields and a Close button. Which step should you implement so keyboard users are not lost?

options.label: Move focus into the dialog on open, trap Tab inside it, and return focus to "Settings" on close
Leave focus on "Settings" so the user's place is kept, and let Tab move through the page behind the dialog
Move focus to the top of the document on open so the dialog is reached in reading order from the start
Remove all tabindex values on the page so Tab skips the background content and lands in the dialog by default

rubric: Focus management moves in, contains, and restores focus.
Leaving focus behind the overlay strands keyboard users; other options don't manage focus.

items.prompt: A screen reader user says a custom dropdown button announces only "button" and never says whether the list is open. The button has `aria-haspopup="listbox"`. What is the most likely missing piece?

options.label: The list needs `role="presentation"` so its items are hidden from the accessibility tree
`aria-haspopup` should be `true` rather than `listbox`, so the popup type is announced
`tabindex="-1"` is missing on the button, so it never receives focus from the keyboard
`aria-expanded` is not toggled as the list opens

rubric: aria-expanded communicates open/closed state.
Other options don't address state announcement.

items.prompt: An audit shows keyboard users can tab to a menu item but cannot see where focus is. The CSS contains `*:focus { outline: 0 }` and a `.menu a:hover { background:#ddd }` rule. What is the root cause?

options.label: The global outline reset removes the focus indicator and no focus style replaces it
The hover rule overrides the browser's tab order, so focus skips the menu items visually
Links only receive keyboard focus when they have an explicit tabindex attribute set
Background colours set in hover rules are ignored by browsers when a keyboard is used

rubric: Removing outlines with no replacement hides focus; hover isn't focus.
Hover doesn't affect tab order; links are natively focusable.

items.prompt:
A tester finds a heading that screen readers skip in the headings list. The markup is `
Pricing
` styled to look like a heading. What explains this?

options.label: Screen readers treat a class named h2 as decoration and skip it when listing headings
The heading text is too short for assistive tech to list it unless it has an aria-label
A div has no heading role, so assistive tech does not expose it as a heading
The styled div needs a lang attribute before screen readers can list it as a heading

rubric: Semantics come from elements or roles, not visual styling.
Class names carry no semantics.

items.prompt: A form field has `<label for="phone">Phone</label>` and `<input id="phone" aria-label="Mobile">`. The screen reader announces "Mobile". Why?

options.label: Screen readers use whichever naming attribute appears last in the source order
aria-label outranks the native label in accessible name computation
aria-label is used only when the associated native label has no text content
The for attribute is ignored whenever the input already has its own id attribute

rubric: aria-label overrides native label content in name computation.
Other options misstate how names are calculated.

items.prompt: A page passes automated contrast checks, yet users with colour blindness cannot tell required fields apart; required fields are only shown with red text labels. Which analysis is correct?

options.label: Meaning is conveyed by colour alone, which fails the use-of-colour criterion even though contrast passes
Passing contrast checks shows the colour requirements are met, so the cause must be the users' display settings
The red text fails contrast because enhanced contrast of 7:1 is required for any text that marks a required field
The labels need a darker shade of red, since a larger contrast ratio would make them distinguishable to these users

rubric: Contrast ratio and use-of-colour are different criteria; add text or an icon.
Automation can't detect colour-only meaning.

items.prompt: A keyboard user reports they get stuck and can't leave a widget. Which findings could cause this trap? Select all that apply.

options.label: The widget uses native `<button>` elements
Focus is moved back into the widget by a blur handler
The widget has `role="group"` with a label
A keydown handler calls `preventDefault()` on Tab inside the widget with no exit key

rubric: Blocking Tab or reclaiming focus creates a trap.
Native buttons and labelled groups don't trap focus.

items.prompt:
A tabs widget works with a mouse. With a screen reader, users hear a list of links with no hint of which is selected, and Arrow keys do nothing. The markup is `
  • One
    • ...
` with JS toggling a `.active` class. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: It lacks tab roles, `aria-selected` state and arrow key handling, so semantics and keyboard pattern are missing
The `.active` class name is not exposed to screen readers, so renaming it to `.selected` will make the state announced
The links are focusable only by Tab, so adding `tabindex="0"` to every list item will supply the missing arrow key support
The list markup is invalid for navigation, so replacing the `ul` with a `div` and `span` set will expose the selected tab

rubric: Tabs need role tablist/tab/tabpanel, aria-selected and arrow keys.
A CSS class doesn't convey state to assistive tech.

items.prompt: A custom menu button is `<div role="button" aria-expanded="false">`. Sighted users see the menu open, but a screen reader always announces it as "collapsed". Which cause is most likely?

options.label: The click handler toggles a CSS class to show the menu but never updates the aria-expanded value
The role="button" attribute overrides aria-expanded, which is only valid on native details elements
The menu items are inside the div, so the screen reader caches the first state it read
The div lacks a tabindex, so the screen reader cannot read any of its ARIA state properties

rubric: ARIA state is not updated automatically; script must change aria-expanded alongside the visual change.
Distractors wrongly treat aria-expanded as invalid on buttons or as an automatically cached value.

items.prompt: A modal dialog opens with a dark backdrop. Mouse users cannot click the page behind it, yet keyboard users pressing Tab move through links hidden under the backdrop. What is the underlying fault?

options.label: The dialog lacks an aria-label, so the browser does not restrict tabbing to its descendants
The backdrop has a lower z-index than the dialog, so keyboard events pass through it to the page
Background content is still focusable because focus is not contained and the page is not made inert
The dialog uses role="dialog", which by design leaves focus order of the page unchanged

rubric: Visual overlays do not block keyboard focus; focus must be trapped or the background made inert.
Distractors blame z-index or naming, which do not control tab order.

items.prompt: A search field shows the visible label "Find products" but has `aria-label="Search"`. Voice-control users saying "click Find products" get no response. Which diagnosis is correct?

options.label: The input lacks type="search", so voice software cannot target it by its visible text
The aria-label is too short, so voice software ignores names under ten characters
The accessible name does not contain the visible label text, so spoken commands cannot match it
The visible label is not inside a fieldset, so voice software cannot associate it with the input

rubric: aria-label overrides the visible text as the accessible name; it should include the visible label (Label in Name).
Distractors invent length, type or fieldset requirements.

items.prompt:
After a failed save, a script inserts `
Save failed
` into the page in one step. Screen reader users hear nothing. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Polite regions only announce text longer than one sentence, so the message was ignored
The aria-live attribute is only honoured on span elements, not on a div
The region and its text were added together, so many screen readers never registered the change
Live regions must use aria-live="assertive", since polite never announces error content

rubric: Live regions are generally best present in the DOM first, then have their content changed.
Distractors invent element or length restrictions or misstate polite behaviour.

items.prompt: Body links are styled only with a blue colour (#0645AD) against black text, with no underline. The blue has a 7:1 ratio against the white background. An audit still flags them. Why?

options.label: Underlines are mandatory on every link under WCAG, so the colour contrast is irrelevant here
Links need 7:1 contrast against the background to meet AA, and blue sits just under that threshold
Colour alone distinguishes the links, and the blue versus surrounding text lacks 3:1 contrast
Links must be a different hue from the surrounding text, whatever the contrast ratio between them

rubric: Colour-only link cues need 3:1 contrast with surrounding text (or another visual cue).
Distractors misstate AA thresholds or claim underlines are always mandatory.

items.prompt: In a single-page app, screen reader users say route changes leave them lost. Which findings help explain the problem? Select all that apply.

options.label: Routes use pushState paths rather than hash fragments in the address bar
Focus stays on the clicked link, which is removed from the DOM, so focus resets to the document start
The app renders its content with client-side JavaScript instead of on the server
document.title stays the same on every route, so there is no cue to the new view
Nothing announces the new view, so users get no cue that the content changed

rubric: Lost focus, silent view changes and a stale title all remove orientation cues.
URL style and client rendering are not in themselves accessibility failures.

items.prompt: A dashboard icon has a tooltip shown only on hover. A screen magnifier user at 400% zoom reports the tooltip vanishes whenever the pointer moves toward it to read it. Keyboard focus never shows it. Which analysis fits best?

options.label: The tooltip is acceptable because hover content is exempt for pointer users who can re-hover
The tooltip needs role="alert" so that magnifier software keeps it visible while the pointer moves
The tooltip fails because its text is under 4.5:1 contrast, which makes magnifiers hide it
The tooltip is not hoverable or focus-triggered, so it cannot be persistently read or dismissed

rubric: Content on hover or focus should be hoverable, persistent and dismissible, and appear on focus too.
Distractors blame contrast, invent an exemption, or misuse role=alert.

items.prompt: A team must build a clickable control. Criteria: works with Enter and Space, exposes button semantics, low maintenance. Which option best meets them?

options.label: A `div` with role="button", tabindex="0", and key handlers for Enter and Space
A native `button` element, styled with CSS to match the design system
An `a` element without href, given role="button" and a click handler
A `span` with an onclick handler and an aria-label describing the action

rubric: Native button provides role, focus and key behaviour without extra code.
Distractors rebuild the behaviour by hand and risk missing parts.

items.prompt: A form field needs extra text that screen readers read but sighted users do not see. It must stay in the accessibility tree and not shift the layout. Which technique is best?

options.label: Set `display:none` on the text so it is removed from the page layout and no longer takes up visual space
Set `visibility:hidden` on the text so it keeps its layout space but is not shown to sighted users
A visually-hidden class using clipping and absolute positioning
Set `font-size:0` and `color:transparent` on the text so that nothing visible remains on screen

rubric: Visually-hidden CSS keeps content available to assistive tech without visual impact.
display:none and visibility:hidden remove it from the accessibility tree; font-size:0 is unreliable.

items.prompt: With one day left, which defect should be fixed first? Criterion: the one most likely to stop users completing a purchase.

options.label: Checkout inputs have no programmatic labels, so screen reader users cannot tell what to enter
Footer copyright text has a 4.4:1 contrast ratio against the background
Decorative hero image lacks an empty alt attribute, so screen readers read its file name
Blog pages jump from an h2 straight to an h4 in a sidebar widget

rubric: Unlabelled checkout fields block the key task entirely.
Other defects are real but have lower impact on task completion.

items.prompt: A vendor claims its one-line overlay script makes any site WCAG 2.2 AA compliant. Criteria: reliability and long-term user outcomes. Which assessment is best?

options.label: Reject it as a substitute for fixing source markup, since it cannot reliably repair structure
Reject it because overlays often interfere with screen reader and keyboard use, so they should never be loaded
Accept it, since automated fixes cover every WCAG success criterion once the script is loaded on the site
Accept it for images only, since overlays can reliably write correct alt text for most images on a page

rubric: Overlays cannot reliably fix semantics, labels and interaction design; fix the source.
Distractors overstate automation or claim overlays always break keyboards.

items.prompt: In code review you see `<nav role="navigation" aria-label="navigation">` as the only nav on the page. Criteria: correct, non-redundant markup. Which comment is best?

options.label: Replace the nav with a div, since an explicit role on a div is more reliable
Add aria-hidden="true" to the nav so the redundant landmark is not announced twice
Remove both attributes; native nav is already a landmark and a lone one needs no name
Keep both attributes, since role is required for older screen readers and the label adds clarity

rubric: Native nav already has the landmark role; a label that repeats the role adds noise.
Distractors preserve redundancy, downgrade semantics, or hide the landmark.

items.prompt: Judge which approaches to form validation errors meet these criteria: errors are announced, tied to their fields, and not conveyed by colour alone. Select all that apply.

options.label: Move focus to an error summary after a failed submit, with links to each invalid field
Include an icon and text such as "Error:" before each message in addition to the red colour
Show errors in red text beside fields and rely on the colour change to flag the problem
Link each error message to its input with aria-describedby and set aria-invalid="true"
Put the error text in a title attribute so it appears when the field is hovered

rubric: Programmatic association, a focus-managed summary and non-colour cues satisfy all three criteria.
Colour-only and title-attribute errors fail to be announced or to be visible to everyone.

items.prompt: A marketing team wants an autoplaying looping background video in the hero. Criteria: users can stop moving content lasting over 5 seconds, vestibular-sensitive users are protected, and the design intent is kept. Which option is best?

options.label: Autoplay muted with a visible pause control, and start paused when prefers-reduced-motion is set
Autoplay with captions added and loop indefinitely, since captions cover the motion requirement
Autoplay muted with no controls, because a silent video cannot cause accessibility barriers
Autoplay and add aria-hidden="true" to the video, so assistive technology does not announce it

rubric: A pause mechanism plus respecting reduced-motion meets both stated criteria.
Muting, aria-hidden or captions do not let users stop motion or protect against it.

items.prompt: A site's main navigation has dropdown sections made of plain links. A developer marks them up with `role="menu"` and `role="menuitem"` for 'richer' semantics. Criteria: match user expectations and avoid needless keyboard cost. Which critique and fix is best?

options.label: Use a button with `aria-expanded` that toggles a list of links, because the menu role promises app-style arrow-key behaviour this nav lacks
Change the outer list to `role="menubar"`, because navigation with several levels needs a top-level role to expose the hierarchy to users
Keep it, because menu roles tell screen reader users the group is navigation and make long link lists faster to scan with arrow keys
Keep the roles and add `aria-haspopup="true"` to every link, because this tells assistive tech each link opens a submenu of its own

rubric: Site navigation is a disclosure pattern; the menu role implies application-menu keyboard behaviour that the page does not implement.
Distractors assume more ARIA means better semantics.

items.prompt: A button shows the visible text `Search` but has `aria-label="Find products"`. Criteria: WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name and support for speech-input users. Which judgment is best?

options.label: Faulty, because a speech user saying 'click Search' won't match the accessible name, which should contain the visible text
Faulty, because `aria-label` is not allowed on buttons, so the name must come from a `title` attribute set to the same text
Acceptable, because speech-input users can say any word from the accessible name and the visible text is not used for matching
Acceptable, because `aria-label` overrides visible text and screen readers announce the clearer name consistently for everyone

rubric: Label in Name requires the accessible name to include the visible label so voice commands work.
Distractors treat aria-label as a free override or invent a restriction on buttons.

items.prompt: White 18px normal-weight text sits over a photographic gradient hero image. The criterion is WCAG AA 4.5:1 wherever the text appears. Which verification approach is most defensible?

options.label: Treat the text as large text and test at 3:1, since a hero heading is visually prominent against the photo
Test against the dominant brand colour in the image, since the rule applies to the colour users notice first
Check contrast at the lightest area behind the text, or add a scrim so the worst case still reaches 4.5:1
Sample the average colour of the image and test it against white, since the average represents what readers mostly see

rubric: Contrast must hold at every point behind text, so the worst case governs, or a scrim guarantees it.
18px normal weight is not large text, and averages hide failing regions.

items.prompt: A toast helper creates a new `div role="status"` and sets its message text in the same step. Testers report screen readers often stay silent. Which critique is best?

options.label: `role="status"` is too weak, so switch the new div to `aria-live="assertive"`, which forces announcement of any inserted node
The message must go in an `aria-label` on the new div, because live regions announce attribute changes rather than text content
Live regions generally must exist in the DOM before their content changes, so keep an empty region and update its text later
Add `aria-atomic="false"` to the new div, because that makes screen readers read the node's content as soon as it is inserted

rubric: Announcements are triggered by changes inside an already-registered live region; injecting region and content together is unreliable.
Distractors reach for stronger politeness or attribute tricks that don't address timing.

items.prompt: In a single-page app, clicking a nav link swaps the view and removes the old one. Focus drops to `body` and screen readers say nothing. Criteria: announce the change, let keyboard users continue from the new content, stay concise. Which approach is best?

options.label: Return focus to the page's skip link on every route change so users always restart from a known place
Leave focus alone and add `role="alert"` to the clicked nav link so its label is repeated after the swap
Update `document.title`, then move focus to the new view's `h1` with `tabindex="-1"` so Tab continues from there
Wrap the whole app in `aria-live="polite"` so each swapped view is read out in full automatically

rubric: Moving focus to the new heading announces the change and sets a sensible keyboard position without reading everything.
Live-region wrapping is verbose, and restarting at the skip link or re-announcing the link doesn't orient users.

items.prompt: An organisation audits a site for WCAG 2.2 AA conformance. Which judgments about audit method are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: Keyboard-only and screen reader walkthroughs are needed alongside tools to catch traps and misleading announcements
One page passing is enough to claim the whole site conforms, since components are shared across templates
A clean automated scan doesn't show conformance, because tools can't judge whether alt text is accurate or focus order is logical
An overlay widget that adjusts contrast and font size makes the underlying markup conformant, so no code audit is needed
A checkout flow must be assessed end to end, because conformance covers complete processes and one failing step fails them all

rubric: Automated tools cover only part of WCAG, conformance applies to complete processes, and manual AT testing is required.
Sampling one page or relying on overlays are common overclaims.

items.prompt: A homepage carousel auto-rotates every 4 seconds. Its slide dots are `div`s and there are no controls, and slides contain links. Criteria: WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide; full keyboard operation; no content lost. Which remedy is best?

options.label: Slow rotation to 12 seconds, which satisfies the pause requirement because users then have enough time to read each slide
Add a real pause `button`, halt rotation while focus is inside, and make the dots buttons so every slide is reachable
Pause rotation on mouse hover only, since pointer users need the extra time and keyboard users can use the dots
Add `aria-live="assertive"` to the carousel so each rotation is announced and users know the content has changed

rubric: Moving content lasting over 5 seconds needs a pause mechanism, and slides must be keyboard reachable.
Slower timing, announcements and hover-only pausing don't meet the requirement.

items.prompt: Design a custom tab widget. Constraints: the tab list is one Tab stop, arrow keys move between tabs, the selected tab is announced, and each tab is tied to its panel. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: A `ul` of anchor links with `aria-current="true"` on the active one, with panels revealed through `:target` so the URL updates and each link points to its panel
`role="tablist"` with `role="tab"` children using `aria-selected` and `aria-controls`, selected `tabindex="0"`, others `-1`, arrows move focus
Buttons all with `tabindex="0"` and `aria-selected`, `aria-controls` pointing to each panel, plus arrow-key handlers that move focus to the next tab button
`role="tab"` buttons using `aria-pressed` toggled on selection, with each panel as `role="region"` and an `aria-labelledby` link back to its tab

rubric: The roving tabindex pattern with tablist, tab, aria-selected and aria-controls gives one tab stop and arrow navigation.
Distractors break the single tab stop, skip arrow keys, or use the wrong state attribute.

items.prompt: Design a skip link. Constraints: it is the first focusable element, becomes visible on keyboard focus, and moves focus to the main content in every browser, not just scroll. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: A hover-only `button` first in the DOM that calls `scrollTo` on the main region, leaving keyboard focus on the button itself
A link with `aria-hidden="true"` placed at the end of the page so only keyboard users meet it after tabbing through everything
A link styled `display:none` that JavaScript reveals on `mouseover`, targeting `<main id="main">` without `tabindex` and relying on scroll
A first-in-DOM `<a href="#main">` moved off-screen until `:focus`, with `<main id="main" tabindex="-1">` so focus lands there

rubric: An off-screen-until-focus link first in the DOM, with a programmatically focusable target, meets all constraints.
Distractors hide the link from keyboards, rely on hover, or only scroll.

items.prompt: Design validation for a signup form. Constraints: errors are found quickly on submit by keyboard and screen reader users, each message is programmatically tied to its field, and errors aren't signalled by colour alone. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: A browser `alert()` that lists the errors, then clears the form so users re-enter data without any colour cues to follow
Red borders and `aria-invalid` on fields, with error text in a `title` attribute, while focus stays on the Submit button
On submit, focus an error summary of links to the fields; each invalid field gets `aria-invalid` and `aria-describedby` to text with an icon
A `role="alert"` message per field, inserted on blur only, in red text with an error icon, and with no `aria-describedby` link between message and input

rubric: A focused summary with links plus described-by messages and non-colour cues covers all three constraints.
Distractors miss association, submit-time discovery or the colour-independence requirement.

items.prompt: Design an icon-only mute toggle. Constraints: the control's name stays stable, its on/off state is exposed programmatically, and it works by keyboard with no custom key handling. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: A `div role="checkbox"` with an icon swap and `title="Mute"`, which exposes state but needs custom Space-key handling
An icon `button` that swaps its SVG and `alt` text only, leaving no programmatic state beyond the changed image
A `button` with fixed `aria-label="Mute"` and `aria-pressed` toggled between true and false so state is exposed without renaming
A `button` whose `aria-label` flips between Mute and Unmute while `aria-pressed` also toggles, so both cues are given

rubric: A native button with a constant name and aria-pressed exposes state with built-in keyboard support.
Flipping the label while also toggling pressed state double-signals and inverts meaning.

items.prompt: Write the focus style for a design system. Constraints: visible on light and dark surfaces, keyboard-only via `:focus-visible`, and still visible in Windows forced-colors mode. Which CSS meets all of them?

options.label: `:focus { background: #eee }`, a tint change that avoids outline overlap with neighbouring elements on both dark and light surfaces
`:focus-visible { outline: none; box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px #000 }`, a thick ring that the browser recolours automatically in forced-colors mode
`:focus-visible { outline: 1px dotted #999 }`, a subtle thin outline that stays faithful to the visual design and is drawn by the browser
`:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid #000; outline-offset: 2px; box-shadow: 0 0 0 2px #fff }`, a real outline that forced colors keep

rubric: A real outline survives forced-colors mode, and the dark outline with a white halo works on light and dark surfaces.
Box-shadow rings are removed in forced colors and thin grey or tint-only styles fail contrast.

items.prompt: Design an autocomplete combobox with a popup listbox where users keep typing while moving through suggestions. Which elements belong in the design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Move DOM focus onto each `option` as arrows are pressed, so the highlighted item is announced natively by the browser
`role="combobox"` on the input with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` pointing at the popup listbox
Give every option `tabindex="0"` so that Tab cycles through the suggestions in order
Keep DOM focus on the input and set `aria-activedescendant` to the id of the highlighted option
Expose the number of results through a polite live region so users learn that suggestions have appeared

rubric: The ARIA combobox pattern keeps focus in the input, uses activedescendant, and announces result counts.
Moving DOM focus into options breaks continued typing, and tabbable options bloat the tab order.

items.prompt: A kanban board lets users drag cards between columns using pointer events only. Constraints: WCAG 2.5.7 needs a non-dragging single-pointer alternative, keyboard users need access, and screen reader users need confirmation of the result. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: Add a 'Move' button on each card opening a menu of columns and positions, then confirm the result in a polite live region
Bind arrow keys on a focused card to simulate dragging motion, moving the card visually without announcing where it ended up
Add `aria-grabbed` and `aria-dropeffect` to cards and columns so assistive technology announces the drag operation as it happens
Add a long-press gesture for touch users and a help link telling keyboard users to contact support to move their cards

rubric: A per-card move menu works by click, tap and keyboard without dragging, and a live region confirms the new position.
Deprecated drag attributes, gesture-only or support-based workarounds, and silent key simulation each miss a constraint.
